App Store Listing in Traditional Chinese — Taiwan & Hong Kong (zh-Hant)

You shipped en-US, maybe added Simplified Chinese for the China storefront — and Taiwan plus Hong Kong still see English or a mainland-flavored page. Traditional Chinese is a separate App Store Connect locale with its own indexed fields, not a character swap from zh-Hans. This page covers why US and EU indie apps miss zh-Hant, what goes wrong when you OpenCC a China listing, and how AppLocale rewrites store copy for Taiwan and Hong Kong while keeping your English product voice. Operator guidance only — no ranking guarantee, not legal advice, and not investment advice.

The zh-Hans gap most indie teams leave open

A common path for US and EU indie apps: launch in English, add Simplified Chinese (zh-Hans) when China traffic shows up, and stop. Taiwan and Hong Kong buyers then hit one of two bad outcomes — an English-only product page that reads foreign, or a zh-Hans localization that Apple may surface with mainland wording (软件, 视频, 信息) and keyword habits that do not match how users search in Taipei or Hong Kong. Neither is a Traditional Chinese listing. Storefront availability for Taiwan and Hong Kong is separate from language rows: confirm both territories are enabled under Pricing and Availability, then add a Chinese (Traditional) localization in Connect — it does not inherit from zh-Hans or en-US automatically.

zh-Hant is its own Connect locale

App Store Connect lists Chinese (Traditional) as a distinct localization row — not a variant of Simplified Chinese and not a regional toggle inside one Chinese row. Taiwan and Hong Kong share the zh-Hant script in Connect, but buyers search with different loanwords, payment vocabulary, and category nouns. Each locale row carries its own title, subtitle, keywords, description, promotional text, What’s New, and screenshot sets. Search indexes zh-Hant fields independently from en-US and zh-Hans. If the Traditional row is empty, Apple falls back to another language — usually English — and you lose indexed zh-Hant terms entirely.

Why OpenCC from Simplified is not enough

OpenCC and similar tools convert characters (软件 → 軟體, 网络 → 網路) but do not rewrite for Taiwan/Hong Kong ASO or buyer expectations. Problems that survive conversion:

  • Search vocabulary — Taiwan users often type different terms than mainland Search (e.g. 影片 vs 视频, 程式 vs 应用, 帳號 vs 账号)
  • Payment and IAP wording — 內購, 訂閱, and 試用 phrasing differs from mainland paywall copy; a converted zh-Hans description can sound like a CN import
  • Subtitle and keyword packing — the 30-character subtitle and hidden keyword field need locale-specific terms, not duplicated visible characters from a converted row
  • Tone and product voice — US/EU indie apps usually want concise, feature-forward English voice carried into zh-Hant, not mainland marketing boilerplate (强大, 专业级) run through a converter
  • Hong Kong vs Taiwan nuance — both use Traditional characters, but colloquial terms and English loanword habits differ; one converted block rarely fits both skims

Character conversion is a starting point for engineers, not a storefront-ready listing. AppLocale writes zh-Hant copy from your English source (and existing zh-Hans only as reference), not as an automated script output.

Taiwan and Hong Kong storefront reality

Both territories pull from the same zh-Hant localization row in Connect today, but user search behavior and payment context diverge. Taiwan Search skews toward local terms and mixed English product names; Hong Kong buyers often tolerate more English in the title but still expect Traditional body copy and IAP labels. US/EU indie apps that never localized beyond en-US leave money on the table in two high-ARPU Chinese markets without touching mainland compliance questions. You do not need a separate app — you need a filled zh-Hant row that reads native on the product page and indexes terms buyers actually type.
